questions.q: What does RESTORE VERIFYONLY actually check?
options: That the database's indexes are not fragmented
That the target restore server has enough disk space
That the backup set is complete, the header is valid, and (with CHECKSUM) page checksums are intact — without performing an actual restore
That the backup, if restored, will bring the database online with no issues
questions.explain: VERIFYONLY is a read-only inspection of the backup file itself — it confirms readability and completeness, not that a full restore will succeed.

questions.q: What does adding WITH CHECKSUM to a BACKUP statement accomplish?
options: It automatically encrypts the backup file
It prevents the backup from ever being restored to a different server
It validates each page's checksum as it's read during the backup, catching corrupt pages before they're silently backed up, and stores a checksum for the backup set itself
It compresses the backup to reduce its size
questions.explain: CHECKSUM catches corruption at the source during the backup and records a checksum that RESTORE VERIFYONLY WITH CHECKSUM can later validate against.

questions.q: By default, what happens when WITH CHECKSUM detects a corrupt page during a backup?
options: The corrupt page is silently skipped with no indication in the backup
SQL Server automatically repairs the corrupt page before continuing
The backup stops, unless CONTINUE_AFTER_ERROR is specified to let it finish anyway (with the result treated as suspect)
The backup succeeds normally with no behavior change
questions.explain: STOP_ON_ERROR is the implicit default; CONTINUE_AFTER_ERROR overrides it but the resulting backup should not be treated as routine.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the only practice that actually proves a backup will bring up a working, queryable database?
options: Checking that the .bak file size matches the database size
Enabling WITH CHECKSUM on every backup
Running RESTORE VERIFYONLY once per backup file
Periodically restoring the backup (and its differential/log chain) to a separate scratch or test instance
questions.explain: Only an actual test restore exercises the full recovery process and proves the backup produces a usable database — VERIFYONLY and CHECKSUM both stop short of that.

questions.q: A backup passes RESTORE VERIFYONLY WITH CHECKSUM cleanly, and a manager concludes it is 'fully verified' with no further checking needed. What's missing from that conclusion?
options: Nothing is missing — VERIFYONLY with CHECKSUM is a complete guarantee of restorability
VERIFYONLY only works on encrypted backups, so this result is meaningless
VERIFYONLY never performs an actual restore, so it can't catch issues like missing target file paths or a broken restore chain that only a real test restore would surface
The backup should have used WITH COMPRESSION instead for a valid check
questions.explain: VERIFYONLY, even with CHECKSUM, is a read-only file-level check — it does not prove the backup will actually restore and recover successfully under real conditions.
